claim: In 100 diagnostic-error cases in internal medicine (autopsy, QA and voluntary reports), errors usually involved both system and cognitive factors; premature closure was the most common single cognitive cause and knowledge deficits were rare.
quote: Diagnostic error is commonly multifactorial in origin, typically involving both system-related and cognitive factors.
authors: Graber ML, Franklin N, Gordon R
title: Diagnostic error in internal medicine
transfer: Errors come from stopping early, not missing facts. Supports a close-out gate that looks for unexplained findings, but only as a conditional step. Case series, no control group, so it shows where errors cluster, not what fixes them. The earlier brief's 74% and 65% figures were not confirmed here.

claim: Telling residents to be slow and reflective did not raise diagnostic accuracy over telling them to be fast (about 44.5% vs 45.0%), though the reflective group took longer per case.
quote: encouraging slowing down and increasing attention to analytical thinking is insufficient to increase diagnostic accuracy.
authors: Norman G, Sherbino J, Dore K, Wood T, Young M, Gaissmaier W, Kreuger S, Monteiro S
title: The etiology of diagnostic errors: a controlled trial of system 1 versus system 2 reasoning
n: second-year residents, 20 cases, two cohorts (Speed 2010, Reflect 2011)
transfer: Do not add a slow-down or always-reflect step to single-answer tasks. Matches our ARC and word-puzzle losses. Note: cohorts were run in different years, not concurrently randomized.

claim: CORRECTION to earlier brief: the PMC link PMC4539330 is Monteiro et al. 2015, not Norman 2014. In that study 47 residents re-reviewed 16 cases; only 8% (60 of 745) of diagnoses were revised and mean score rose just from 1.20 to 1.22 of 2.
quote: Only 8 % of diagnoses were revised resulting in a small but significant increase in scores
authors: Monteiro SD, Sherbino J, Patel A, Mazzetti I, Norman GR, Howey E
title: Reflecting on diagnostic errors: taking a second look is not enough
transfer: A self-directed second look rarely changes the answer and rarely finds the error (only 18% of fully wrong first diagnoses were revised). A self-review step without new information is nearly a no-op, so give the second pass new input (a rival, a check).

claim: Differential-diagnosis checklist that contained the correct diagnosis raised student accuracy to 0.75 vs 0.49 control; a checklist without the correct diagnosis gave 0.43; a prompt only gave 0.53. Only the checklist with the correct answer differed from control.
quote: Students using a DDXC that contained the correct diagnosis had better diagnostic accuracy
authors: Kämmer JE, Schauber SK, Hautz SC, Stroben F, Hautz WE
title: Differential diagnosis checklists reduce diagnostic error differentially: a randomised experiment
transfer: A list of alternatives helps only if it holds the right answer. A candidate-generation step needs an independent source of candidates; measure gold-in-candidates recall. One small study, students.

claim: Systematic review of 28 studies on dual-process interventions: guided reflection was the most consistently successful (across five studies) and cognitive forcing improved accuracy and confidence judgements; measures were heterogeneous and samples mostly early-career.
quote: guided reflection interventions emerged as the most consistently successful across five studies
authors: Lambe KA, O'Reilly G, Kelly BD, Curristan S
title: Dual-process cognitive interventions to enhance diagnostic reasoning: a systematic review
transfer: Structured reflection (compare findings against each hypothesis) beats a bare 'think again'. Use a fixed template with the evidence in view, not a generic doubt prompt.

claim: Review of causes of errors: educational strategies aimed at recognizing biases did not reduce errors, while strategies that reorganize knowledge showed small but consistent benefit; biases can be induced in the lab but their real-world share is unclear.
quote: Educational strategies directed at the recognition of biases are ineffective in reducing errors
authors: Norman GR, Monteiro SD, Sherbino J, Ilgen JS, Schmidt HG, Mamede S
title: The causes of errors in clinical reasoning: cognitive biases, knowledge deficits, and dual process thinking
transfer: Do not rely on 'name the bias and avoid it' prompts. Put effort into retrieval of structured knowledge (cards, scripts) instead. Narrative review by the main skeptics of the bias-first view.

claim: Debiasing checklist and knowledge-retrieval (content) checklist did not significantly beat control on ECG interpretation; more errors occurred on bias-inducing cases.
quote: Diagnostic performance under either checklist intervention was not significantly better than the control.
authors: Sibbald M, Sherbino J, Ilgen JS, Zwaan L, Blissett S, Monteiro S, Norman G
title: Debiasing versus knowledge retrieval checklists to reduce diagnostic error in ECG interpretation
transfer: CORRECTION to earlier brief: it recalled that knowledge-retrieval helped more; the abstract says neither checklist beat control overall (novices may gain). Treat both as unproven. Small n.

claim: Systematic review: 20 studies with 6,810 physicians linked overconfidence, anchoring, information bias and availability bias to diagnostic errors; only two studies looked at patient outcomes and most studies were low quality.
authors: Saposnik G, Redelmeier D, Ruff CC, Tobler PN
title: Cognitive biases associated with medical decisions: a systematic review
venue: BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making 16:138
transfer: Bias-error link is common but evidence is weak on outcomes. Anchoring is a real target for a blind-second-opinion step, but do not claim effect sizes. Systematic review without pooled effect. Summary seen via fetch, not verbatim.

claim: Outpatient diagnostic errors occur at about 5.08% of US adult visits or episodes, about 12 million adults a year, about half potentially harmful.
quote: a rate of outpatient diagnostic errors of 5.08%
authors: Singh H, Meyer AN, Thomas EJ
title: The frequency of diagnostic errors in outpatient care: estimations from three large observational studies involving US adult populations
transfer: none (base rate for the field; shows why the field cares). Useful only as context.

claim: In a vignette study, 118 internists were right on 55.3% of easier cases but only 5.8% of difficult cases, while mean confidence barely changed (7.2 vs 6.4 of 10).
authors: Meyer AN, Payne VL, Meeks DW, Rao R, Singh H
title: Physicians' diagnostic accuracy, confidence, and resource requests: a vignette study
transfer: Stated confidence is a poor signal of correctness. Do not gate on the model's self-reported confidence; use disagreement across independent calls or an external check.

claim: Overconfidence is a documented cause of diagnostic error: physicians underestimate how often their diagnoses are wrong.
authors: Berner ES, Graber ML
title: Overconfidence as a cause of diagnostic error in medicine
transfer: Same lesson as diag-a-10: calibration needs outside signals. Summary only from a database record.

claim: Reflection improved accuracy on cases similar to earlier cases (availability bias) among internal medicine residents, compared with non-analytical reasoning; second-year residents scored lower on cases resembling earlier ones (1.55 vs 2.19).
authors: Mamede S, van Gog T, van den Berge K, Rikers RM, van Saase JL, van Guldener C, Schmidt HG
title: Effect of availability bias and reflective reasoning on diagnostic accuracy among internal medicine residents
n: residents, year 1 and year 2 groups; exact n not confirmed
transfer: Structured reflection (list features for and against each candidate) can undo recency anchoring after a similar earlier case. Candidate for a step when the context holds a similar prior case or lesson card.

claim: Reflection helped on complex cases and made no difference on simple ones; non-analytical reasoning matched reflection on routine cases; no overall main effect.
authors: Mamede S, Schmidt HG, Penaforte JC
title: Effects of reflective practice on the accuracy of medical diagnoses
transfer: Supports a router: reflect only when the case is hard, skip on easy ones. This is the human version of our result that doubt hurts when the first answer is usually right.

claim: Across 393 clinicians (students, trainees, faculty), instructions to be fast or analytic made no accuracy difference (F[1,379]=2.44, P=.12); vignette complexity and experience had large effects.
authors: Ilgen JS, Bowen JL, McIntyre LA, Banh KV, Barnes D, Coates WC, Druck J, Fix ML, Rimple D, Yarris LM, Eva KW
title: Comparing diagnostic performance and the utility of clinical vignette-based assessment under testing conditions designed to encourage either automatic or analytic thought
transfer: Replicates diag-a-02 in a larger sample: mode instructions do not matter, case difficulty and knowledge do. Do not tune a schema on 'speed' prompts.

claim: Structured reflection improved delayed test performance (0.66 vs 0.48 and 0.52) but scored lower on the immediate test (0.48 vs 0.62 for differential-diagnosis group) in students learning diagnostic competence.
authors: Mamede S, van Gog T, Moura AS, de Faria RM, Peixoto JM, Rikers RM, Schmidt HG
title: Reflection as a strategy to foster medical students' acquisition of diagnostic competence
transfer: Reflection pays through learning, not through the immediate answer. For an agent, the value is in writing a lesson card for later problems, not in the current answer.

claim: Illness-script review: the concept has solid theoretical underpinnings, explains how expertise develops and led to the Script Concordance Test.
authors: Custers EJFM
title: Thirty years of illness scripts: theoretical origins and practical applications
transfer: Cards with enabling conditions, key features and look-alikes per problem class. Mostly theory and recall studies; no strong accuracy effect sizes.

claim: A randomized trial of an illness-script workshop for students found about 14% higher scores on clinical reasoning problems, but similar overall diagnostic thinking scores to controls.
authors: Lee A, Joynt GM, Lee AK, et al.
title: Using illness scripts to teach clinical reasoning skills to medical students
transfer: Weak support for script cards. URL is a search link, not the paper; treat as unverified beyond a database summary.

claim: Randomized trial: 50 physicians with GPT-4 access scored 76% vs 74% with conventional resources (adjusted difference 2 points, 95% CI -4 to 8, P=.60); GPT-4 alone scored 92%.
quote: did not significantly improve clinical reasoning compared with conventional resources.
authors: Goh E, et al.
title: Large language model influence on diagnostic reasoning: a randomized clinical trial
transfer: The model alone beat humans with the model: value comes from a program that runs the model, not advice to a reader. LLM-alone comparison was exploratory.

claim: GPT-4 on 70 NEJM clinicopathologic cases had the correct diagnosis in its differential in 64% (45/70) and as top diagnosis in 39% (27/70).
quote: provided the correct diagnosis in its differential in 64% of challenging cases and as its top diagnosis in 39%.
authors: Kanjee Z, Crowe B, Rodman A
title: Accuracy of a generative AI model in a complex diagnostic challenge
transfer: Verifies the earlier brief's 64%. A gap between 'in the list' and 'top of list' (64 vs 39) shows ranking, not generation, is the weak step: a step that picks the discriminating check could use that gap. Research letter, no control.

claim: BiasMedQA (1,273 USMLE questions with seven cognitive biases): average accuracy drop under bias was -5.1% for GPT-4, -17.8% for GPT-3.5, -20.1% for Llama 2 70B; bias education gave +3.5% to +6.5% for most models and did not restore accuracy.
quote: improved but did not fully restore accuracy
authors: Schmidgall S, Harris C, Essien I, et al.
title: Evaluation and mitigation of cognitive biases in medical language models
transfer: Smaller models are more anchorable; false consensus bias hurt most (24.9% average drop). Our wrong-card and leading-hint controls should be measured. Bias education helped LLMs a little, unlike humans.

claim: AMIE, a conversational diagnostic AI, was rated superior on 30 of 32 axes by specialists and 25 of 26 by patient-actors in a study with 159 scenarios and 20 primary care physicians.
quote: AMIE demonstrated greater diagnostic accuracy and superior performance on 30 out of 32 axes
authors: Tu T, Schaekermann M, Palepu A, et al.
title: Towards conversational diagnostic artificial intelligence
transfer: AMIE used a self-play, multi-stage reasoning design, but the abstract does not isolate which stage drives the gain. Simulated text consults, not real patients.

claim: Hypothetico-deductive model: clinicians generate a small set of hypotheses early from the first cues and then gather data to test them; the right hypothesis must be generated early.
authors: Elstein AS, Shulman LS, Sprafka SA
title: Medical Problem Solving: An Analysis of Clinical Reasoning
transfer: Loop: generate 3 to 5 candidates early, choose the datum that separates them, update. I did not open the book this session; the 3 to 5 figure is from memory.

claim: MAI-DxO, an orchestrated panel around o3, reported about 80% accuracy on 304 NEJM sequential-diagnosis cases vs about 20% for physicians working without references, with cost tracked; no independent replication or equal-compute ablation seen.
authors: Nori H, et al. (Microsoft AI)
title: Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models
venue: arXiv preprint (not peer reviewed as far as I know)
transfer: Best public example of a differential + test-choice + cost schema. A fetch of Europe PMC returned no record, so figures are from memory and the earlier brief. Authors' own benchmark; check structure vs compute before copying.
